## 1. Traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 1:** Jehoram's father, Jehoshaphat, was a godly king. But Guzik says one of the worst things Jehoshaphat did was arrange for Jehoram to marry Athaliah, the daughter of Ahab and Jezebel (he points to 2 Kings 8:16–18, 26). The full harm of this only showed after Jehoshaphat died.

**v. 2:** Why is Jehoshaphat called "king of Israel"? Guzik quotes Poole, who gives several possible reasons:
- he was rightfully king of Israel;
- many Israelites from the north had settled in his kingdom;
- all his subjects were Israelites, even though he didn't rule all Israel;
- or, as some say, a copyist wrote "Israel" where the original had "Judah."

**v. 3:** Jehoshaphat gave his other sons gifts and fortified cities. Guzik sees this as a wise policy copied from Rehoboam (2 Chronicles 11:18–23). Spreading the sons around the country, away from the capital, meant they couldn't band together against the heir.

**v. 4:**
- Even with that precaution, Jehoram killed all his brothers so none of them could threaten his rule.
- Selman (quoted by Guzik) says that "strengthened himself" here clearly means violently removing every other possible claim to the throne, including some leading officials.
- Dilday (quoted) notes that the Jewish historian Josephus says Athaliah urged Jehoram to commit the murders.
- Guzik adds that some may have hoped the royal marriage would lift up the northern kingdom spiritually. Instead it dragged Judah down.

**v. 6:**
- "The ways of the kings of Israel" is no compliment. Judah had a mix of good and bad kings, but Guzik says Israel's kings were all evil.
- Clarke (quoted) calls Athaliah notorious for ungodliness and cruelty, like her mother, and thinks she was probably the main cause of Jehoram's cruelty.

**v. 7:**
- The verse implies that Jehoram's evil deserved destruction, but God held back because he was faithful to his covenant with David.
- Wiseman (quoted) says the "lamp" is more than a picture of life and witness: it reminded hearers of the covenant (Psalm 132:17).
- Payne (quoted) notes that God's promise to David wasn't formally called a "covenant" when first given (2 Samuel 7; 1 Chronicles 17). Later passages do call it that (2 Samuel 23:5; Psalm 89:3, 34; Psalm 132:11–12).

**v. 8:** Edom had been a client kingdom paying tribute to Judah. Seeing Judah's weakness under Jehoram, it broke free.

**v. 9:** The text doesn't say how the night battle ended, and Guzik thinks it may have been indecisive. Edom's continued revolt shows Judah didn't regain control.

**v. 10:**
- Guzik takes Edom's revolt as proof that Jehoram's kingdom was weak. He thought the alliance with Ahab's house would strengthen Judah, but his disobedience weakened it, "because he had forsaken the LORD."
- Selman (quoted) says nothing else is known about Libnah's revolt. Libnah was a town of uncertain location on Judah's western border, near Lachish.
- F. B. Meyer (quoted) observes that Judah's kings kept the surrounding nations in check while they stayed loyal to God. When they turned from God, the nations turned from them.
- Guzik applies this to everyday life. When we submit to God, our passions stay under our control; when we stop, they flare up. The same goes for authority in the home, church and government: it is safe to submit to leaders who are themselves submitted to God.

**v. 11:**
- Jehoshaphat (2 Chronicles 17:6) and Asa (2 Chronicles 14:1–5) worked against the high places. Jehoram promoted them.
- Selman (quoted) says Jehoram was the first king of Judah to actually build high places, probably including a temple of Baal in Jerusalem (compare 2 Chronicles 23:17).
- Guzik gives two reasons idolatry is called "prostitution." Pagan fertility worship often involved sex with temple priests or priestesses. And Israel owed God the faithfulness a wife owes her husband, so idolatry was spiritual adultery.

**v. 12:** How could Elijah send a letter, when he seems to have been taken to heaven during Jehoshaphat's reign (2 Kings 2; 3:11)? Guzik gives two answers:
- Poole (quoted) offers two options. The writer may have been Elisha or another prophet called "Elijah" because he came in Elijah's spirit, as John the Baptist did. Or, the option Poole prefers, Elijah really wrote it, foreseeing Jehoram's reign by the Spirit.
- Payne (quoted) suggests Elijah may have died before the letter was delivered, so its sentence of doom came like a voice from the dead.

Guzik also notes that Elijah's main ministry was to the northern kingdom, so this message to a king of Judah is unusual.

**v. 13:**
- God's main charge is that Jehoram followed his father-in-law Ahab rather than his father and grandfather.
- "Better than you" means God saw the murdered brothers as more worthy to rule than Jehoram.

**v. 15:** The bowel disease is announced as God's punishment for Jehoram's sins.

**v. 16:** The attack by the Philistines and Arabs is a further judgment, God raising up enemies to trouble his reign.

**v. 17:** Guzik sees fitting justice here. Jehoram killed his brothers to protect his throne, and he lost all but one of his own sons. Payne (quoted) says the man who began by massacring his brothers ended by losing his sons and wives.

**v. 18:** The disease is fitting too. Jehoram was rotten inside spiritually, and God made his body match his soul. Clarke (quoted) says the Targum (an ancient Aramaic paraphrase) hints at constipation and inflammation before the bowels finally burst.

**v. 19:**
- Trapp (quoted) calls the two years of suffering a foretaste of eternal punishment unless Jehoram repented.
- Selman (quoted) says translation problems make this verse harder. Following Keil and Dillard, he suggests the end may have come suddenly, "in two days," rather than after two years.

**v. 20:**
- Knapp (quoted) calls Jehoram one of Judah's most unlovely kings. His name means "exalted by the LORD," yet his wickedness brought him to a dishonoured grave.
- Clarke (quoted) notes that no historian is named as recording his life.
- G. Campbell Morgan (quoted) observes that people follow those who lead them into evil out of selfishness, never out of love. Love is only inspired by goodness.

## 2. Where Protestant traditions differ
I found nothing. Enduring Word (Calvary Chapel / Pentecostal-leaning) was the only tradition I could check.

## 3. Other views (modern scholarship, Catholic/Orthodox, popular modern teaching)
I found nothing. The only modern-scholarship point I have is the one Guzik reports from Selman and Dillard on v. 19 ("two days" vs. "two years").
